questions.learningObjective: Define external political efficacy in a transit context
questions.stem: A transit board member asks riders whether their input changes route decisions.

options.text: The belief that government responds to citizen input.
The number of riders who actually attend meetings.
The belief that officials ignore all public feedback.
The legal right to vote in transit elections.

questions.explanation: External efficacy is the belief that government responds; option C states the opposite belief, so it is wrong. The other options confuse efficacy with participation or rights.
questions.hint: Efficacy is about belief in responsiveness.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: A rider keeps backing the same transit party despite route cuts.

answer.exemplar: Party identification is a durable psychological attachment to a party that persists even when policy outcomes disappoint, shaping vote choice beyond immediate interests.

questions.explanation: Party ID acts as a standing decision rule; it survives short-term policy losses. The tempting view that voters simply chase outcomes misses this attachment.
questions.hint: Think of party ID as a long-term attachment.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Calculate free riders in a transit group
questions.stem: A transit coalition has 120 members but only 45 pay dues; how many free ride?
questions.explanation: Subtract paying members from total members: 120 minus 45 equals 75 free riders. The tempting error is to report the paying count instead.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify agenda setting in a transit debate

stimulus.body: The board only discusses fare hikes after a newspaper series. Riders never see bike lanes on the docket. The chair sets topics each month.

questions.stem: Which concept best describes the chair choosing monthly topics?

options.text: Agenda setting by the chair controlling discussion topics.
options.misconception: confuses agenda setting with voting rules

options.text: A binding referendum on all transit decisions.
A random lottery selecting which riders speak.
An automatic legal mandate requiring debate.

questions.explanation: The chair selecting topics is agenda setting. The other options mistake discussion control for voting, lotteries, or mandates.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: A petition with 8,000 signatures forces a transit vote; 6,200 riders later approve it.

options.text: The petition stage is the initiative, the vote is referendum.
The petition is a veto and the vote is a recall.
The vote is an initiative and petition is referendum.

questions.explanation: Citizens propose via initiative, then voters decide via referendum. Option A captures this; others collapse or reverse the stages.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Predict boycott effect on transit revenue
questions.stem: A boycott cuts daily ridership from 4,000 to 2,800 for 5 days; lost trips?
questions.explanation: Daily loss is 1,200 trips times 5 days equals 6,000 lost trips. The tempting error multiplies total ridership by days.
questions.hint: Find daily loss first, then multiply by days.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Wealthy riders vote at higher rates in transit elections than poor riders.

answer.exemplar: Turnout rises with socioeconomic status, so higher-income riders participate more, creating a gradient that skews transit policy toward their preferences.

questions.explanation: Higher status predicts higher turnout, biasing outcomes. The tempting error assumes turnout is uniform across classes.
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Riders must register 30 days early at a single downtown office with limited hours.

options.text: A policy of free transit for all riders.
A registration deadline and location barrier.
A random lottery for route assignments.
A guaranteed seat on every bus.

questions.explanation: Early deadlines and distant offices are administrative barriers. The others describe benefits or unrelated mechanisms.
questions.hint: What makes voting harder to complete?
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Recognize strategic voting in a transit race

stimulus.body: Maria prefers the Green Line party but votes for the Red Line party to stop the Blue Line party. Her true preference is unchanged.

questions.stem: What behavior does Maria display?

options.text: Sincere voting for her top preference.
Strategic voting to block a worse outcome.

questions.explanation: Maria votes for a second choice to prevent a worse result, which is strategic voting. The others mislabel the behavior.
questions.hint: Is she voting her true preference?
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

questions.learningObjective: Classify a cleavage by social base
questions.stem: Urban renters and suburban homeowners split sharply over transit funding.

options.text: A class cleavage between capital and labor.
A territorial cleavage between city and suburb.

questions.explanation: The split follows geography, a territorial cleavage. The others import class, religion, or ethnicity not present.
questions.hint: What social line divides the groups?
questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT

provenance.author: bank-team-comparative-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Over a decade, transit riders shift from one party to another en masse.

answer.exemplar: Party realignment is a durable, large-scale shift of voters from one party coalition to another, reshaping the party system for years.

questions.explanation: Realignment is durable and large-scale, not a temporary swing. The tempting error treats any vote shift as realignment.
questions.hint: Is the shift durable and large-scale?

questions.stem: A transit advocacy group raises funds and recruits volunteers to lobby the board.

options.text: A media blackout on transit news.
A spontaneous uprising with no organization.
A court ruling forcing transit changes.
Resource mobilization gathering money and people for action.

questions.explanation: Gathering funds and volunteers is resource mobilization. The others describe spontaneity, courts, or censorship.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Advocates link fare equity to family budgets and fairness. Riders adopt the language and join the campaign.

questions.stem: What process connects advocacy language to rider participation?

options.text: A budget cut to transit services.
Frame alignment linking issues to shared values.

questions.explanation: Linking issues to shared values is frame alignment. The others are unrelated processes.

questions.stem: Transit riders only read news that favors their preferred line.

answer.exemplar: Selective exposure is choosing information that confirms prior views, reinforcing existing transit preferences and filtering out contrary evidence.

questions.explanation: People seek confirming information, not balanced coverage. The tempting error assumes riders consume all viewpoints equally.
questions.hint: Do riders seek confirming or opposing news?

questions.stem: After surveillance cameras are installed, fewer riders attend board meetings.

questions.stem: Two transit parties split votes 50/50; what is the effective number?
questions.explanation: With two equal parties, the effective number is 2. The tempting error uses raw party count without weighting.
questions.hint: Equal split means effective number equals count.

questions.stem: A city has many rider clubs, unions, and neighborhood groups tied to transit.

questions.explanation: Many organizations mean high associational density, boosting engagement. The tempting error counts only voters, not groups.

Insider lobbying using personal access to officials.
A consumer boycott of the line.
A random citizen lottery for input.

questions.explanation: Private access by a former insider is insider lobbying. The others are outsider tactics or unrelated.

questions.stem: Negative ads about a transit candidate air for two weeks before the election.

options.text: No effect on any group's turnout.
Turnout always doubles for all groups.
Turnout may rise among opponents and fall among supporters.

questions.explanation: Attack ads can mobilize opponents and demobilize supporters. The others overstate, deny, or absurdly restrict effects.

questions.stem: A transit lobbyist knows rider data that officials lack.

questions.explanation: Unequal information lets lobbyists steer outcomes. The tempting error assumes officials always know as much.

A new social movement emphasizing post-material values.

Electoral access reforms expanding how people vote.

questions.stem: Transit news reaches riders through community leaders who interpret it.

questions.stem: After winning a transit seat, the movement's volunteers stop organizing.

answer.exemplar: Post-victory demobilisation is the decline of movement activity after achieving its goal, as participants disengage once the win is secured.

questions.explanation: Victory reduces urgency and activity. The tempting error assumes movements keep mobilizing after winning.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Only angry riders speak at board meetings, skewing perceived opinion.

questions.stem: Younger riders favor transit expansion in every survey year.

options.text: A period effect from one election.
Pure age effect that fades with time.
A cohort effect tied to generation.

questions.explanation: Consistent generational preference is a cohort effect. The others misattribute it to aging, period, or noise.

The color of the rider's pass.

answer.exemplar: Free riding happens when benefits are non-excludable, so individuals gain without contributing, undermining collective action.

questions.explanation: Non-excludable benefits let non-contributors gain. The tempting error blames laziness rather than incentives.

options.text: The chair can suppress issues despite public support.
The board has no authority over fares.
